lessons.title: Structural Sections, Form & Melody
lessons.description: Song sections, musical forms, scales, intervals and melodic devices.
lessons.content_html:
Building Blocks of Music

Understanding musical structure, form and melody is essential for analysing and creating music. This lesson covers the structural sections that make up a song, the standard forms used to organise them, and the scales, intervals and devices that shape a melody.

Structural Sections

Most songs are built from a set of recognisable sections, each with a specific function:

  • Intro — the opening section that establishes the mood, tempo and key before the vocals enter.
  • Verse — tells the story. The melody usually stays the same, but the lyrics change each time.
  • Pre-chorus — a short section that builds tension and anticipation before the chorus.
  • Chorus — the main hook of the song. It has the most memorable melody and repeats with the same lyrics and music.
  • Bridge — a contrasting section that provides variety and prevents the song from becoming repetitive.
  • Outro — the ending section, often a fade-out or a final statement of the chorus or theme.
  • Middle 8 — an eight-bar section in the middle of the song that introduces new musical material.
  • Refrain — a repeated line or phrase, often at the end of a verse (shorter than a full chorus).
  • Coda — a concluding passage that brings the music to a definitive end (from the Italian for “tail”).
  • Breakdown — a stripped-back section where instruments drop out, common in electronic and dance music.
  • Drop — the moment after a build-up when the full beat and bass return with maximum energy (common in EDM).
  • Riser — an ascending sound or build-up that creates tension before a drop or chorus.
Key Fact

The twelve structural sections you need to know are: intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, outro, middle 8, refrain, coda, breakdown, drop and riser. Each has a distinct role in the song.

Musical Form

Form describes how sections are arranged to create the overall structure of a piece. The spec requires you to know seven forms:

  • Through-composed — no repeated sections. The music is different throughout. Common in art songs and film scores.
  • AAA (strophic) — the same music repeats for every verse. Simple and repetitive, often used in folk songs and hymns.
  • AB (binary) — two contrasting sections, A and B. Each is usually repeated (AABB).
  • ABA (ternary) — three sections where the first section returns at the end. The B section provides contrast.
  • ABCBA (arch) — a symmetrical structure that mirrors itself. Sections move away from the opening and then return.
  • ABACA (rondo) — the A section keeps returning between contrasting episodes (B, C, etc.).
  • 12-bar — a repeating 12-bar chord progression using three chords (I, IV, V). The foundation of blues, rock and roll and many pop songs.

Melody: Scales

Melodies are built from scales. Each scale has a specific pattern of intervals (tones and semitones) that gives it a distinctive character.

  • Major scale — T, T, S, T, T, T, S. Sounds bright and happy.
  • Natural minor scale — T, S, T, T, S, T, T. Sounds sad or melancholic.
  • Harmonic minor scale — T, S, T, T, S, T+S, S. The raised 7th note creates a distinctive “exotic” sound and a strong pull back to the root.
  • Minor pentatonic scale — T+S, T, T, T+S, T. Five notes, widely used in blues, rock and pop melodies.
  • Major pentatonic scale — T, T, T+S, T, T+S. Five notes, bright and open-sounding. Common in folk and pop.
Key Fact

Major: T,T,S,T,T,T,S. Natural minor: T,S,T,T,S,T,T. Harmonic minor: T,S,T,T,S,T+S,S. Minor pentatonic: T+S,T,T,T+S,T. Major pentatonic: T,T,T+S,T,T+S.

Melody: Intervals & Devices

An interval is the distance between two notes. Diatonic intervals stay within the notes of the scale. Chromatic intervals use notes outside the scale (sharps and flats not in the key).

Composers use melodic devices to develop melodies:

  • Retrograde — playing the melody backwards (reversing the note order).
  • Inversion — turning the melody upside down. If the original goes up a step, the inversion goes down a step.

Melodic form describes the shape of a melody:

  • Arch — the melody rises to a peak and then falls back down.
  • Repetition — the same phrase or motif is repeated, often with small variations.
  • Sequences — a melodic pattern is repeated at a higher or lower pitch.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on structure and form often give you a scenario (e.g. “A song has an intro, two verses with different lyrics but the same melody, a chorus that repeats, and a bridge”) and ask you to identify the form or describe the sections. Learn the letter labels: A = first section, B = contrasting section. For scales, memorise the tone/semitone patterns — they are frequently tested in multiple-choice and short-answer questions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Songs are built from structural sections (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, etc.) — know all twelve for the exam.
  • Musical forms organise sections into patterns: through-composed, strophic (AAA), binary (AB), ternary (ABA), arch (ABCBA), rondo (ABACA) and 12-bar.
  • Melodies are built from scales (major, natural minor, harmonic minor, minor pentatonic, major pentatonic) and shaped by devices (retrograde, inversion) and melodic forms (arch, repetition, sequences).

practice_questions.text:
Which musical form features a repeating A section between contrasting episodes?
A) Binary (AB)
B) Ternary (ABA)
C) Rondo (ABACA)
D) Strophic (AAA)
practice_questions.marks: C — Rondo (ABACA) (1 mark). In rondo form, the A section returns between contrasting B, C episodes.

practice_questions.text: Identify two structural sections commonly found in electronic dance music.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: breakdown (1), drop (1), riser (1), intro (1), outro (1). Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe the interval pattern of the harmonic minor scale and explain what makes it different from the natural minor scale.
practice_questions.marks: The harmonic minor scale pattern is T, S, T, T, S, T+S, S (1). It differs from the natural minor by having a raised 7th note (1). This creates the distinctive T+S interval between the 6th and 7th notes, giving the scale an 'exotic' sound and a strong pull back to the root note (1). 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between the verse and the chorus in a typical pop song structure.
practice_questions.marks: The verse tells the story and the lyrics usually change each time it appears (1), while the melody stays the same or similar (1). The chorus is the main hook of the song with the most memorable melody (1) and it repeats with the same lyrics and music each time, making it the most recognisable part (1). 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the use of different musical forms affects the listener's experience of a piece of music. Refer to at least two forms in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis of at least two forms with clear explanation of their effect on the listener.
Mid band (3-4): Sound analysis of at least one form with some listener impact.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification.
Indicative content: Strophic (AAA) — familiarity and accessibility through repetition, but can become predictable; rondo (ABACA) — balance of repetition and variety, the returning A section provides familiarity while contrasting episodes maintain interest; through-composed — keeps the listener engaged with constant development but no repetition to anchor to; ternary (ABA) — satisfying sense of return when A comes back; 12-bar — strong rhythmic drive, predictable harmony allows for improvisation.

practice_questions.text: A composer wants to write a melody for a sad, atmospheric piece of music. Discuss which scale they might choose and how they could use melodic devices to develop their melody.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion of scale choice with justified reasoning and detailed application of multiple melodic devices.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good scale choice with some development using devices.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Appropriate scale identified with basic use of a device.
Lower band (1-2): Limited response.
Indicative content: Scale choice — natural minor (T,S,T,T,S,T,T) for a sad, melancholic feel; harmonic minor for a darker, more exotic atmosphere; minor pentatonic for a simpler, blues-influenced mood. Melodic devices — retrograde (play melody backwards for variation), inversion (turn melody upside down for contrast). Melodic form — arch shape (rise to an emotional peak and fall), sequences (repeat motifs at different pitches for development), repetition (anchor the listener with a recurring phrase). Credit any justified combination.

lessons.title: Harmony, Rhythm & Instrumentation
lessons.description: Chord types, time signatures, rhythmic devices and acoustic and electronic instruments.
lessons.content_html:
Harmony, Rhythm & Instrumentation

This lesson covers the final three musical elements you need for the exam: harmony (chords and progressions), rhythm (time signatures, devices and tempo) and instrumentation (acoustic and electronic instruments, plus DJ technology).

Harmony

Harmony is created when two or more notes sound together. The building blocks of harmony are chords.

Chord Types

You need to know seven chord types:

  • Major — sounds bright and happy. Built from root, major 3rd, perfect 5th.
  • Minor — sounds sad or dark. Built from root, minor 3rd, perfect 5th.
  • Diminished — sounds tense and unstable. Built from root, minor 3rd, diminished 5th.
  • Augmented — sounds unsettled and dreamlike. Built from root, major 3rd, augmented 5th.
  • Minor 7th — a minor chord with an added minor 7th. Warm, jazzy character.
  • Major 7th — a major chord with an added major 7th. Smooth, sophisticated sound.
  • Suspended (sus) — replaces the 3rd with a 2nd (sus2) or 4th (sus4), creating an unresolved, open sound.
Key Fact

Seven chord types: major (bright), minor (sad), diminished (tense), augmented (dreamlike), minor 7th (jazzy), major 7th (smooth) and suspended (unresolved). Know the character of each — this helps with analysis questions.

Chord Progressions

A chord progression is a sequence of chords that forms the harmonic backbone of a piece. Progressions can be:

  • Diatonic — using only chords built from the notes of the key. These sound natural and expected.
  • Chromatic — using chords that include notes from outside the key. These create surprise, tension or colour.

Rhythm

A time signature tells you how many beats are in each bar and what note value represents one beat.

Simple time — each beat divides naturally into two equal parts:

  • 2/4 — two crotchet beats per bar (marches, polkas)
  • 3/4 — three crotchet beats per bar (waltzes)
  • 4/4 — four crotchet beats per bar (most pop, rock, hip-hop)
  • 5/4 — five crotchet beats per bar (irregular, unsettling feel)
  • 6/4 — six crotchet beats per bar
  • 7/4 — seven crotchet beats per bar (progressive rock)

Compound time — each beat divides naturally into three equal parts, giving a swinging, lilting feel:

  • 6/8 — two dotted-crotchet beats per bar (jigs, some ballads)
  • 9/8 — three dotted-crotchet beats per bar
  • 12/8 — four dotted-crotchet beats per bar (slow blues, gospel)

Rhythmic Devices

Rhythmic devices add interest and groove to music:

  • Syncopation — placing accents on weak beats or off-beats, creating a sense of surprise and groove. Common in funk, jazz and pop.
  • Triplets — three notes played in the time of two, creating a flowing, rolling feel.
  • Dotted rhythms — a dot after a note adds half its value, creating a long-short pattern that gives energy and drive.

Tempo

Tempo is the speed of the music, measured in BPM (beats per minute). A slow ballad might be 60–80 BPM, a pop song 100–130 BPM, and a fast dance track 140–180 BPM. Tempo changes (accelerando for speeding up, rallentando for slowing down) add expression and drama.

Instrumentation

Instrumentation refers to which instruments are used in a piece. The spec divides instruments into acoustic, electronic and DJ technology.

  • Strings — plucked (guitar, harp, banjo) or bowed (violin, viola, cello, double bass).
  • Percussion — tuned (timpani, xylophone, vibraphone) or untuned (snare drum, bass drum, cymbals, tambourine).
  • Keyboards — piano and organ.
  • Brass — valved (trumpet, French horn, tuba) or slide (trombone).
  • Woodwind — flutes (flute, piccolo) or reeds (clarinet, oboe, bassoon, saxophone).
  • Vocals — lead vocals (main melody and lyrics) and backing vocals (harmonies and support).

Electronic instruments:

  • Electric guitar and electric bass — use pickups and amplifiers to produce sound.
  • Synthesiser — generates sound electronically using oscillators, filters and envelopes.
  • Sampler — plays back recorded audio samples triggered by keys or pads.
  • Drum machine — produces electronic or sampled drum sounds, programmed into patterns.

DJ technology:

  • Turntables — play vinyl records, allowing scratching and beat-matching.
  • CDJs — CD or USB-based players used by DJs for digital music playback.
  • Mixer — blends audio from multiple sources with crossfader, EQ and effects.
  • DJ software — applications like Traktor or Serato that provide virtual decks, effects and beat-matching tools on a laptop.
Key Fact

Acoustic instrument families: strings (plucked and bowed), percussion (tuned and untuned), keyboards (piano, organ), brass (valved and slide), woodwind (flutes and reeds), vocals (lead and backing). Know examples from each category.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the exam, you may be asked to identify instruments from a description or audio extract, or to explain the difference between simple and compound time. For harmony questions, remember: diatonic = within the key, chromatic = outside the key. For instrumentation questions, make sure you can classify any given instrument into its correct family and sub-category (e.g. clarinet = woodwind, reed).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Harmony is built from seven chord types (major, minor, diminished, augmented, minor 7th, major 7th, suspended). Progressions can be diatonic or chromatic.
  • Rhythm uses simple time (beats divide into 2) and compound time (beats divide into 3). Devices include syncopation, triplets and dotted rhythms.
  • Instrumentation covers acoustic families (strings, percussion, keyboards, brass, woodwind, vocals), electronic instruments and DJ technology.

practice_questions.text:
Which chord type sounds tense and unstable, and is built from a root, minor 3rd and diminished 5th?
A) Major
B) Augmented
C) Diminished
D) Suspended
practice_questions.marks: C — Diminished (1 mark). A diminished chord is built from root, minor 3rd and diminished 5th and sounds tense.

practice_questions.text: Identify two examples of compound time signatures.
Describe what syncopation is and explain why it is used in music.
practice_questions.marks: Syncopation places emphasis on beats or parts of beats that are normally weak (1). This creates a sense of rhythmic surprise or groove (1). It is commonly used in genres like funk, jazz and pop to make the rhythm feel more energetic and interesting (1). 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between simple time and compound time, giving an example of each.
practice_questions.marks: In simple time, each beat divides naturally into two equal parts (1). An example is 4/4, which has four crotchet beats per bar (1). In compound time, each beat divides naturally into three equal parts, giving a swinging or lilting feel (1). An example is 6/8, which has two dotted-crotchet beats per bar (1). 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a producer could use different chord types to create contrast between a verse and a chorus.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis of specific chord choices with clear explanation of their emotional effect and how they create contrast.
Mid band (3-4): Sound analysis of chord use in at least one section.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of chord types.
Indicative content: Verse — minor chords for a reflective or melancholic mood, possibly minor 7ths for a jazzy, complex feel; suspended chords for an unresolved, searching quality. Chorus — major chords for brightness, energy and resolution; shift from minor to major creates emotional contrast. Chromatic chords between sections add surprise. Diatonic progressions give a natural, stable feel while chromatic progressions create tension.

practice_questions.text: A producer is creating a track that combines acoustic and electronic instruments. Discuss the instruments they could use and explain how the combination could affect the overall sound and character of the track.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion of multiple instruments from both categories with detailed explanation of how they interact.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good coverage of instruments from both categories with some analysis of combination.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some instruments identified from both categories.
Lower band (1-2): Limited response.
Indicative content: Acoustic — piano for harmonic foundation, acoustic guitar for strummed or fingerpicked parts, strings (bowed) for emotional depth, vocals for melody and lyrics. Electronic — synthesiser for pads or leads, drum machine for programmed beats, sampler for textural elements, electric bass for low-end. Combination effects — warmth of acoustic + precision of electronic, natural dynamics + programmed rhythms, blending timbres for unique sound. DJ technology could add live performance elements. Credit any justified combination with explanation of sonic character.

lessons.title: Musical Styles & Technology Through the Decades
lessons.description: How musical styles evolved alongside recording technology from the 1950s to today.
lessons.content_html:
Musical Styles & Their Defining Elements

Over the last seven decades, popular music has transformed dramatically. Each new style brought distinctive musical elements — and each decade saw new technology that made those styles possible. Understanding the link between style and technology is essential for this qualification.

Every musical style can be described using the same building blocks: structural sections (verse, chorus, bridge), form (how sections are ordered), melody, harmony, rhythm, and instrumentation. As you study each decade, notice how these elements change alongside the available technology.

Key Fact

The eleven styles you must know are: rock and roll (1950s), folk and rock and soul (1960s), funk, disco, and reggae (1970s), hip hop and electronica (1980s), dance (1990s), and 21st century pop (2000s).

1950s — Rock and Roll

Rock and roll emerged as one of the first truly youth-oriented musical styles. Its defining elements include a strong backbeat on beats 2 and 4, simple verse-chorus form, blues-influenced melody, and basic three-chord harmony (I–IV–V).

Instrumentation centred on the electric guitar, electric bass, drums, and vocals. The key technology was 2-track recording, which allowed artists to record a backing track on one track and vocals on another. This was a huge leap from single-take live recording.

1960s — Folk, Rock & Soul

Folk used acoustic guitar, simple strophic form (repeating verse melody), and storytelling lyrics. Rock built on rock and roll with louder amplification, extended instrumental sections, and more complex song structures. Soul fused gospel-influenced vocals with rhythm and blues, using call and response and rich horn sections.

The 1960s introduced 4-track and 8-track recording, meaning multiple instruments could be layered on separate tracks and mixed independently. Hardware effects like tape delay, reverb chambers, and tremolo became common in studios. Analogue synthesis also appeared, allowing producers to create entirely new electronic timbres.

1970s — Funk, Disco & Reggae

Funk is built on syncopated bass lines, tight rhythmic grooves, and a strong emphasis on beat one. Disco features a steady four-on-the-floor kick drum, lush string arrangements, and a driving tempo around 120 BPM. Reggae has an offbeat “skank” guitar rhythm, prominent bass, and a laid-back tempo.

Technology in the 1970s included the drum machine, continued development of analogue synthesis, and the move to 16-track and 24-track recording. More tracks meant greater layering and more complex arrangements.

1980s — Hip Hop & Electronica

Hip hop introduced rapping (rhythmic speech) over sampled breakbeats, with DJs scratching vinyl and looping existing recordings. Electronica relied almost entirely on electronic instruments — synthesisers, drum machines, and sequencers — creating repetitive, layered textures with few or no acoustic instruments.

Key Fact

The 1980s saw five major technological developments: the digital sampler (recording and replaying short audio clips), digital tape (higher quality recording), digital synthesis (computer-generated sounds), MIDI (a protocol allowing electronic instruments and computers to communicate), and the Portastudio (an affordable home multitrack recorder).

MIDI was introduced in 1983 and became a universal standard. It does not transmit audio — it transmits performance data (which note, how hard, how long). This meant a single musician could control multiple synthesisers, drum machines, and effects from one keyboard. MIDI laid the foundation for the computer-based music production that dominates today.

1990s — Dance

Dance music in the 1990s encompassed sub-genres like house, techno, trance, and drum and bass. Common elements include a four-on-the-floor beat, synthesised bass lines, sampled vocals, and build-and-drop structures designed for nightclub DJs to mix together.

Two key technologies of the 1990s were hard disk recording and the keyboard workstation. Hard disk recording allowed producers to record, edit, and arrange audio on a computer screen — a fundamental shift from tape-based workflows. The keyboard workstation combined sounds, sequencing, and effects in one device, making music production more portable.

2000s — 21st Century Pop

21st century pop blends elements from many earlier styles. It often features programmed beats, auto-tuned vocals, layered synthesisers, and hook-driven melodies. Song structures vary but tend to prioritise the chorus as the most memorable section.

The dominant technology is the DAW (Digital Audio Workstation), which puts a full recording studio inside a laptop. Audio processing plug-ins replicate effects like reverb, compression, and EQ in software. At the same time, there has been an analogue hardware revival — producers deliberately use vintage analogue equipment or software emulations of classic gear to achieve the warmer sound of earlier decades.

Key Fact

Decade-by-decade technology summary: 1950s — 2-track recording. 1960s — 4/8-track, hardware effects, analogue synthesis. 1970s — drum machine, analogue synthesis, 16/24-track. 1980s — digital sampler, digital tape, digital synthesis, MIDI, Portastudio. 1990s — hard disk recording, keyboard workstation. 2000s — DAW, plug-ins, analogue revival and software emulation.

Technology and style are closely linked. Multitrack recording made layered arrangements possible, which helped soul and rock develop their complex sounds. The drum machine enabled the repetitive grooves of disco and funk. The digital sampler allowed hip hop producers to borrow and rearrange existing recordings. Hard disk recording and DAWs made electronic dance music accessible to bedroom producers, leading to an explosion of sub-genres in the 1990s and 2000s.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In extended response questions, you may be asked to describe the musical elements of a style and explain how technology made it possible. Always link the technology to the style — for example, explain that hip hop relies on the digital sampler because producers looped existing recordings to create new beats. Use precise terminology (e.g. “four-on-the-floor”, “syncopated bass line”) rather than vague descriptions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Eleven musical styles span the 1950s to the 2000s, each with distinctive elements of melody, harmony, rhythm, structure, and instrumentation.
  • Recording technology evolved from 2-track tape in the 1950s through multitrack, MIDI, and digital sampling to modern DAWs with plug-ins.
  • Each technology advance directly enabled new musical styles — the digital sampler enabled hip hop, hard disk recording enabled dance music, and the DAW enabled 21st century pop production.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following technologies was introduced in the 1980s?
A) 2-track recording
B) Hard disk recording
C) MIDI
D) DAW
practice_questions.marks: C — MIDI (1 mark). MIDI was introduced in 1983 as a universal protocol for electronic instruments.

practice_questions.text: Identify two musical elements that define the disco style.
practice_questions.marks: 1 marks for each correct element (max 2): four-on-the-floor kick drum (1), lush string arrangements (1), driving tempo around 120 BPM (1), synthesised bass lines (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the key differences between 1960s rock and 1950s rock and roll in terms of musical elements and technology.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per valid point (max 3): Rock used louder amplification (1). Rock had more complex/extended song structures (1). Rock had extended instrumental sections (1). Technology moved from 2-track to 4-track and 8-track recording (1). Hardware effects like tape delay became common (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the introduction of MIDI in the 1980s was significant for music production.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explanation with reasoning (max 4): MIDI allowed electronic instruments and computers to communicate (1). It transmits performance data, not audio (1). One musician could control multiple synthesisers and drum machines from a single keyboard (1). It laid the foundation for computer-based music production and DAWs (1). It became a universal standard used across all manufacturers (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the development of recording technology from the 1950s to the 1980s directly influenced the musical styles that emerged in each decade.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis across multiple decades showing clear cause-and-effect between technology and style. E.g. 2-track recording in the 1950s limited arrangements to simple overdubs, suiting rock and roll’s stripped-back sound. 4/8-track in the 1960s enabled layered soul arrangements with horn sections. 16/24-track and drum machines in the 1970s supported the complex grooves of funk and the repetitive patterns of disco. The digital sampler in the 1980s directly enabled hip hop by allowing producers to loop existing recordings.
Mid band (3-4): Some analysis with links between technology and style, but less detailed or covering fewer decades.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about technology or style with limited connection between the two.

practice_questions.text: To what extent has the development of digital technology since the 1990s changed the way music is produced compared to earlier decades? In your answer, refer to specific technologies and musical styles.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive response comparing analogue/tape-based production with digital production. References hard disk recording, DAWs, plug-ins, and software emulation. Links to dance music and 21st century pop. May discuss the analogue revival as a counterpoint. Well-structured argument with clear examples.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good comparison with several specific technologies and styles. Mostly well-structured with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points about digital technology with limited comparison to earlier methods. Fewer specific examples.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about digital technology with little or no comparison or specific examples.

glossary_terms.definition: The combination of rhythm, melody, harmony, instrumentation, and structure that gives a genre its recognisable sound.
A style originating in the 1950s combining blues, country, and gospel, characterised by a strong backbeat, electric guitar riffs, and energetic vocals.
An early recording method where audio was captured on two separate tracks, allowing basic overdubbing and stereo separation.
Outboard audio devices such as reverb units, tape delay, and tremolo that physically alter the signal before it reaches the recorder.
A method of generating sound electronically using oscillators, filters, and amplifiers, producing waveforms rather than sampling real instruments.
An electronic instrument that generates rhythmic patterns automatically, replacing or supplementing a live drummer.
Musical Instrument Digital Interface — a standard protocol introduced in 1983 that allows electronic instruments, computers, and other devices to send and receive musical data.
Recording audio directly to a computer hard drive rather than to tape, enabling non-destructive editing, cut-and-paste, and instant playback.
A hardware synthesiser that combines sound generation, sequencing, and effects processing in a single unit.
Digital Audio Workstation — software such as Logic Pro, Ableton Live, or Pro Tools that allows recording, editing, mixing, and mastering on a computer.
